stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Dr. Benjamin Spock, The Common Sense Book of Baby and Child Care (1946). Spock told parents to trust their own judgment, writing that 'you know more than you think you do.' He called child-rearing a natural process and urged a relaxed, permissive approach instead of strict schedules and harsh discipline.

stem: Spock's book became a bestseller in part because it appeared at the same time as which development?

options.text: The sharp decline of the birth rate after the war ended
options.misconception: Background from the books: births rose sharply after the war, in the baby boom, so the birth rate did not decline.

options.text: A government program that raised children in nurseries
options.misconception: Background from the books: no government nursery program raised children in the 1950s.

options.text: The baby boom that filled new suburbs with young children
A return to strict Victorian rules for raising children
options.misconception: Spock's book urged the opposite of strict Victorian rules, so it did not ride on their return.

rationales.A: Background from the books: births rose sharply after the war, in the baby boom, so the birth rate did not decline.
rationales.B: Background from the books: no government nursery program raised children in the 1950s.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the book appeared in 1946, just as the baby boom began, so millions of new parents needed its advice at once.
rationales.D: Spock's book urged the opposite of strict Victorian rules, so it did not ride on their return.
rationales.general:
1. Background from the books: the book appeared in 1946, the first year of the postwar baby boom.
2. Background from the books: births rose to a peak of about 4.3 million in 1957, so millions of new parents needed advice at once.
3. A reassuring book that told parents to trust themselves met that need exactly.
Remember: A book sells when it answers a need that millions of people feel at the same time.
